data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories inevitably smuggles induction back into Popper's system because any practical application of corroboration implicitly assumes the uniformity of nature.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper can define a form of rationality that does not rely on expectations of future stability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference can be shown to be purely retrospective with no forward-looking implications.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'acting on' a theory can be decoupled from expecting it to work.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"While Popper formally denies that corroboration implies probability, the act of preferring one theory over another for the purpose of action (prediction, engineering, policy) logically requires the assumption that the patterns observed in the past (survival of tests) will hold in the future. Without this inductive bridge, the preference is arbitrary. The 'critical attitude' itself relies on the expectation that falsification is a meaningful concept over time, which presupposes a stable reality.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
